title: Contract Composition
story: A banking system transferred $10,000 from account A to account B — but account B's balance became negative because it had an overdraft fee that wasn't checked. A composed contract would have caught the cascade of failures before the transfer executed.
why: When multiple types with contracts interact, the composed contracts form a safety net that catches errors at any depth of the call chain.
analogy: Contract composition is like interlocking gears — each gear (type/function) has its own teeth (contracts), and when they mesh, the whole machine turns smoothly or jams immediately on misalignment.
try_it: Add a `close_account` function that takes `Account` by value (move) and returns the final balance. This consumes the account — after close, it can never be used again. Add an `ensures` that the returned balance equals the input balance.
tips: When a function takes multiple contract-protected types, list all preconditions — don't rely on downstream checks
Pass by value (move) when the function should CONSUME the argument — prevents use-after-merge
Chain `@pre` references carefully — `a@pre.balance` refers to a's balance before ANY mutation in this function
common_mistakes: Using `b.balance` in ensures after modifying `b` — but since `b` is consumed (move), post-state checks on it are meaningless
Forgetting that both Account invariants must hold at function exit — the compiler checks `from.balance >= 0` and `to.balance >= 0`
Passing both accounts by `&mut` when one is consumed — pick the right ownership for each parameter
